## Project timeline

How the project got here — from an empty repository to the first release, in
plain language. Every step landed as a tested pull request; every claim was
verified by running it, not by writing it down.

**Early October — the paper stage**

- **The project is born** with a full product requirements document — the whole
  design written down before any code: what the firewall does, how it is built,
  and how every promise will be proven.
- The governance scaffolding lands the same week: contribution guide, security
  policy, code of conduct, CI pipelines, badges, and the project website.

**8 October — the first building blocks work**

- **The design document ships to the public** as the project's specification.
- **The rule engine boots** — the first command runs a security rule against a
  test request and returns a verdict, exactly as the design promised.
- **The kernel shield's first program compiles, loads and detaches cleanly** in
  the Linux lab — the eBPF test environment is real.

**9 October — data starts flowing**

- **Test cases verified for the packet path** — the ring buffer feeding events
  from the kernel to the engine passes its end-to-end check in the lab.
- **The inspection ladder appears** — requests are scored stage by stage, with
  verdicts recorded at every step.
- **HTTP request parsing** lands: the engine now reads real web traffic into a
  clean, rule-friendly view.

**10 October — v0.1, one big day**

- **Dev lab demo done** — a Kubernetes lab boots on demand, the gateway routes
  real traffic through the firewall, and each hop is proven with response
  headers anyone can reproduce.
- **Test cases verified against the real world** — the engine's verdicts match
  the industry-standard rule set (ModSecurity's OWASP CRS) on every test case,
  with the comparison enforced on every future change.
- **Policy files now do something** — a policy written as Kubernetes YAML is
  compiled and loaded, and the affected traffic is actually blocked; the full
  round trip is timed well under the five-second budget.
- **The ban engine enforces in the kernel** — repeat offenders get dropped at
  wire speed, bans expire on their own, and every ban leaves a written record.
- **Every verdict leaves three correlated records** — a trace, a counter and a
  log line, tied together by request id.
- **Bot detection's first cut** — a curl request and a browser request produce
  clearly different fingerprints, verified against published test vectors.
- **Positive security's first cut** — a route's API schema becomes an
  allow-list: requests a schema can't describe get rejected, naming exactly
  which field broke the contract.
- **The honest exit** — the README now states what exists and what does not,
  the exit checklist is run and referenced, and the whole thing ships as
  **v0.1.0, a signed release** with the lab evidence attached.

## Roadmap

Work is tracked on the [Trishula — Roadmap board](https://github.com/orgs/trishula-dev/projects/1) (org Project) as issues [TR-01 … TR-41](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues) in the `trishula` repo. Every issue lands a runnable artefact with an exit criterion — prove the ladder end-to-end, not slide-by-slide.

| Milestone | Items | Status |
|---|---|---|

## Sprint sequencing

The v0.1 sprint sequence: shield PoC → ingest → ladder slice → NGF steering lab → CRS differential → operator/CRD round-trip → ScoredWindowBan → OTel pipeline → bot v0 → positive security v0 → honest exit ([TR-14](https://github.com/trishula-dev/trishula/issues/14)).

## Contributing

Contributions follow the [contributing guide](contributing.html): pick an issue labeled `complexity:starter` or any `area:*` that suits you; the referenced PRD section in the issue body is the design source. Branch + PR against `trishula-dev/trishula` (MIT).
